Sensorium: An Open-Source Multimodal Data Collection and Curation Library for Embodied Surgical AI

Lorenzo Mazza Email: lorenzo.mazza@nct-dresden.de    Ariel Rodriguez Email: ariel.rodriguezjimenez@nct-dresden.de    Stefanie Speidel
Abstract

Embodied surgical AI requires reliable multimodal data, yet surgical data collection remains costly, difficult to repeat, and strongly dependent on the hardware setup. We present Sensorium, an open-source Python library for recording, processing, annotating, and curating multimodal surgical data from configurable robot and sensor streams using the Robot Operating System (ROS) and ROS 2 middleware. The library combines operator-facing data acquisition, configurable processing, semantic annotation, and episodic dataset generation. We evaluate Sensorium across 1,516 recordings of phantom, ex vivo, and in vivo porcine experiments involving multiple surgical tasks and sensing configurations, and report preliminary usability feedback.

††footnotetext: †Corresponding authors. 1NCT/UCC Dresden, UKDD Dresden, TU Dresden, DKFZ Heidelberg. 2BMFTR Research Hub 6G-Life. 3Cluster of Excellence CeTI. 4HZDR Dresden.

1 Introduction

Recent progress in embodied surgical AI has increasingly relied on multimodal recordings of surgical activity, including video, robot kinematics, and semantic annotations. This trend is reflected in the emergence of multimodal surgical datasets [5, 17], which facilitate a range of learning paradigms and applications, from behavioral cloning for surgical task automation [13, 12, 6, 16, 18, 2], to surgical vision-language models [20, 14, 9, 27, 8] and generative surgical world models [7, 23].

However, acquiring such multimodal data and annotations in surgical settings is particularly expensive [4]. Data collection protocols require clinical input, clinicians have limited availability, and in vivo experiments require substantial preparation, coordination, and ethical approval. Recording tools must therefore support reliable acquisition and preserve data for reuse with different representations, sampling rates, and annotation protocols. Scarcity and limited repeatability also make usability a central requirement of the recording process: operators need clear indications of sensor readiness and recording state, along with immediate episode review before the experimental setup changes. The infrastructure should also accommodate varying robot and sensor interfaces across laboratories. This diversity is evident when looking at platforms used for surgical robotics research, including da Vinci Research Kit (dVRK) [11], KUKA robotic platforms [22], Franka Emika Panda [10], and UR5/UR5e [21, 19], as well as in Open-H-Embodiment Dataset [17], which aggregates data from a large variety of commercial, research, and custom robotic platforms.

Recent open-source multimodal data acquisition systems address parts of these requirements. SurgSync [28] provides timestamp-aligned acquisition recording of robot kinematics, stereo endoscopic video, and additional sensing on the dVRK, together with tools for post-processing and annotation. Its acquisition stack and hardware integration are designed around the dVRK and its associated sensing setup. MiDAS [26] is a framework targeted for robotic platforms that do not expose robot telemetry: it employs external electromagnetic and RGB-D tracking, and foot-pedal sensing to approximate robot kinematics. This leaves a gap for a general-purpose framework that directly records heterogeneous robot and sensor data while supporting their processing and annotation for embodied surgical AI systems.

To address this gap, we present Sensorium, an open-source Python library for collecting, processing, annotating, and curating multimodal surgical data for embodied AI applications. Sensorium integrates custom sensor modalities through ROS and ROS 2, and provides both a command-line interface and a browser-based graphical interface (GUI) for local and remote operation. The library includes tools for timestamp-based temporal alignment and stereo rectification, together with annotation functionalities for surgical phases [24, 3] and language instructions for language-conditioned surgical robot learning [12, 6]. Additionally, Sensorium organizes recordings into reusable episodic datasets and supports both raw CSV-based representations and the widely adopted LeRobot format [1, 17], facilitating their use across different surgical AI pipelines, including policy learning, vision-based force estimation, and world model training. Sensorium has been deployed as the recording application of an open-source laparoscopic robotics testbed [19], where it was used to collect a dataset of surgical robot demonstrations for bowel grasping and retraction on phantom and ex vivo [16, 25]. It was also used to record two in vivo porcine datasets covering endoscope guidance, tissue grasping, and tissue retraction, which were subsequently included in [17].

In summary, our contributions are the following:

  • •

    An open-source, flexible, configuration-driven library for collecting and curating multimodal recordings from heterogeneous ROS-integrated surgical sensors and robots.

  • •

    An operator-oriented browser GUI that unifies recording supervision, episode review, surgical-phase and language annotation, and dataset generation.

  • •

    A real-world validation of the library across phantom, ex vivo, and in vivo porcine data-collection settings, complemented by preliminary usability feedback.

The library code is available at 11 1 https://github.com/nct-tso-robotics/tso_sensorium.

2 System Overview

Sensorium organizes multimodal surgical data collection around episodes, as illustrated in Figure 2. Acquisition runs alongside the robotic system through ROS and stores each recording as a raw episode containing timestamped video and state streams. Subsequent curation, processing, annotation, and dataset export are ROS-independent and can therefore be performed later on a separate workstation. Validated configuration files define both the streams acquired during recording and how raw episodes are subsequently processed and exported.

2.1 Multimodal Acquisition

Sensorium acquires heterogeneous data streams through the ROS middleware. Any device that exposes its measurements as a ROS topic can be added through configuration, without modifying the recording core. Across our deployments, this enabled acquisition from stereo endoscopes, pedal boards, haptic input devices, force sensors, and robotic platforms, as well as calibrated robot–camera transformations. In our deployments, the clocks of all workstations running the robot, camera, and other sensors are synchronized using the Precision Time Protocol (PTP). The recorder always preserves the publication timestamp present in each ROS message header. Complete ROS bag recording can optionally be enabled to retain the original message streams. Starting a recording creates a self-contained raw episode containing the selected video and state streams. The browser recording interface, shown in Figure 2a, provides a live camera view and displays the availability of configured sensor streams, the recording state, and the elapsed episode time. Before acquisition begins, required streams and the output location are checked, allowing recording failures to be detected while the experimental setup can still be inspected or corrected. Once an episode is stopped, it is finalized and becomes immediately available for review.

2.2 Curation and Processing

The curation interface in Figure 2b can run either as part of the recording application or independently over an existing recording directory. Users can browse video streams and divide an episode into temporal segments using a dataset-configurable phase-to-language mapping. Each phase can be associated with multiple paraphrased language instructions, increasing textual diversity in the recorded data. A single segment or dataset-level task description can instead provide a global instruction for coarse-grained tasks. These annotations provide aligned textual and categorical phase annotations, supporting language-conditioned policy learning [6], surgical VLM training [9, 2, 14], and surgical phase supervision [3, 24, 16]. For data processing, selected streams are first restricted to their common temporal interval and aligned to a configurable reference stream using nearest-neighbor timestamp matching. For each reference timestamp tit_{i}, the closest sample from stream kk is selected as

ji(k)=arg​minj⁡|ti−tj(k)|.j_{i}^{(k)}=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{j}\left|t_{i}-t_{j}^{(k)}\right|.

Episodes exceeding a configurable alignment tolerance are rejected. Configurable transformations can then be applied to the aligned data, including stereo rectification, resizing, and coordinate-frame transformations. Because these operations are performed after acquisition, different representations can be generated from the same raw episode.

2.3 Dataset Construction and Export

After alignment and processing, a configurable episodic schema defines the observations, robot states and actions, and textual/categorical annotations included in the final dataset. Phase and language annotations are projected onto the aligned timeline and stored alongside the selected sensor and robot data. Sensorium currently supports two export formats: per-episode CSV tables with optional losslessly encoded PNG frames or LeRobot v3 datasets containing Parquet-backed features and image or video observations [1]. For LeRobot export, actions can be selected from recorded sensor streams or derived from observations, with optional magnitude-based filtering to suppress small action fluctuations (Figure 3). Appendix C provides an example configuration, including observation/action mappings and filtering thresholds. Each episode is validated independently before export, so recordings that do not satisfy the configured alignment or schema requirements are excluded and reported without interrupting construction of the remaining dataset.

Demonstration plan.

We will demonstrate episode review, surgical-phase and language annotation, action filtering, and LeRobot export through Sensorium’s browser interface using previously collected surgical recordings. A prerecorded video will illustrate data acquisition on the robotic platform, allowing the complete workflow to be presented without requiring surgical hardware at the workshop.

3 System Evaluation

We evaluate Sensorium along three dimensions: deployment breadth across surgical tasks and experimental settings, temporal consistency of the constructed episodes, and preliminary usability for experiment operators.

Deployment breadth and downstream use.

Overall, the system was used for 1,516 recordings using the UR5e robotic platform from [19], spanning demonstrations and policy rollouts in phantom, ex vivo, and in vivo 22 2 All procedures were approved by the local state authority (redacted for anonymity) and conducted in accordance with institutional ethical standards for animal experimentation and the registered protocol. settings. Table 1 summarizes the recorded cohorts and sensing modalities: the recordings comprise 13 h 04 min of data across bowel grasping and retraction, endoscope guidance, liver lifting, thread pulling, tissue displacement, and open-surgery bowel retraction. They include combinations of stereo video, robot state, gripper state, pedal input, force sensing, IMU measurements, and camera–robot transformations. As a downstream validation, datasets collected and curated using Sensorium were used to train the behavioral cloning policies evaluated in [16, 18] and the vision-based force-estimation models evaluated in [25]. Recordings have also been used for preliminary world-model training in ongoing research. This demonstrates the complete pipeline from heterogeneous hardware to surgical AI training data.

Temporal alignment.

We evaluated the timestamp-alignment procedure by measuring the nearest-neighbor residual between each reference-camera timestamp and its associated sensor-state samples. As shown in Table 1, the median residual was at most 8.60 ms across all cohorts, while the 95th percentile remained at most 17.68 ms.

Preliminary operator usability.

Additionally, seven users of Sensorium provided preliminary feedback through an eight-item 5-point Likert questionnaire [15] (1: strongly disagree, 5: strongly agree). Overall ease of use, integration into the procedural workflow, visibility of sensor readiness, and willingness to use the system in future recording sessions all received a mean score of 5.0/5. Starting and stopping recordings, identifying when recording was active, and confidence that data were saved received 4.86/5. Open-ended responses highlighted the simplicity of the recording interface, rapid access to recorded episodes, and remote operation. Suggested improvements included recording shortcuts, clearer feedback during saving, and additional separation between episode-deletion controls. More details are presented in Appendix A.

4 Conclusion

We presented Sensorium, an open-source Python library for recording data from ROS-based sensors and devices, annotating and curating recordings, and exporting them into datasets ready for downstream AI applications, including policy learning, world models, and vision-based force estimation. Limitations include the need to wrap sensors without native ROS support in ROS nodes, dataset export being tied to the selected reference stream without support for resampling to a user-defined frequency, and a user evaluation limited to seven participants from a single laboratory, restricting the generalizability of the usability findings to other workflows and hardware configurations. Future work will focus on evaluating Sensorium across different robotic platforms, experimental setups, and research sites, and on extending the library based on feedback from the broader community. We hope that its open-source release facilitates wider adoption and contributes to more reproducible and accessible data collection workflows for robotics and AI.

Appendix A User Feedback

Seven users from a single laboratory completed an eight-item questionnaire using a 5-point Likert scale (1: strongly disagree; 3: neither agree nor disagree; 5: strongly agree). Table 2 reports the responses using anonymous respondent identifiers. All seven respondents consented to quotation of their anonymized feedback in a publication.

Error-message ratings.

Both respondents who selected 3 had experienced no recording errors. Their neutral ratings therefore reflect the absence of an opportunity to assess error messages during recording.

Open-ended feedback.

Respondents highlighted the straightforward interface, accessible recording list, ease of starting and stopping recordings, rapid removal of unwanted episodes, and access to recording and review from devices on the local network. One response identified slight uncertainty during saving. Suggestions included a keyboard shortcut, voice control for starting and stopping recordings, and greater spacing between episode rows to reduce accidental deletion. One respondent reported needing a brief explanation of the interface; four reported no required assistance, and two left that question unanswered. These observations are preliminary feedback from a small, single-laboratory sample.

Appendix C Configuration Pseudocode

The following pseudocode summarizes the endoscope guidance configuration, showing its selected topics and observation/action mappings. Executable configurations are included in the accompanying codebase ZIP. The export names below follow the LeRobot writer.

record:
  stereo   <- "/stereo/camera_driver/image_raw"
  robot    <- "/ur5e_rcm_twist_controller/RobotState"
    fields: relative_tip_position, relative_pivot_RPY
  rotation <- "/robot_camera_transform"
    fields: transform.rotation.{x, y, z, w}

for each episode:
  align streams by nearest timestamp over their common interval
    reference: stereo; tolerance: 0.1 seconds
  left, right <- deinterlace, resize(960, 540), rectify(stereo)
  phase, language <- join annotations with the configured phase legend
  displacement <- xyz(robot.relative_tip_position)
  roll <- first_component(robot.relative_pivot_RPY)
  R <- rotation_matrix(rotation)  # camera-to-robot-base rotation

  for i = 0, ..., number_of_aligned_rows - 2:
    state[i] <- concat(inverse(R[i]) * displacement[i], roll[i])
    translation[i] <- inverse(R[i]) *
                      (displacement[i+1] - displacement[i])
    roll_change[i] <- wrap_to_[-pi, pi)(roll[i+1] - roll[i])
  discard the terminal row, which has no successor

over all successfully assembled episodes:
  zero translation vectors below the 30th percentile of nonzero norms
  zero roll changes below the 20th percentile of nonzero magnitudes

export each retained row i:
  observation.images.left  <- left[i]              RGB[540, 960, 3]
  observation.images.right <- right[i]             RGB[540, 960, 3]
  observation.state <- state[i]                    float32[4]
  action <- concat(translation[i], roll_change[i])  float32[4]
  task_phase <- phase[i]                           int64[1]
  task metadata <- language[i] or the default task description

The state vector contains the recorded relative tip displacement expressed in the current camera frame, followed by the recorded roll. Actions are derived next-sample translation and wrapped roll increments. Denoising changes only the action components without overwriting raw data, and its computed thresholds are saved in dataset metadata.
